name: Tommo So
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: McPherson, Laura. 2013. A Grammar of Tommo So. (Mouton Grammar Library 62.) Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. [p. 66 read as publisher-preview; pp. 9, 67-68 as scan; pp. 43, 52, 86 as Google Books search excerpt]. Corroborated by McPherson, Laura. 2010. A Grammar of Tommo-So, Dogon Language Family, Mali. Draft 9/28/10, UCLA, sec. 3.2.2 'Metrical structure', pp. 15-16 (open the Internet Archive copy).
catalog_locator: Ch. 3 'Segmental phonology', sec. 3.6 'Metrical structure', p. 66, continuing in sec. 3.6.1 'Vowel reduction' pp. 66-67; summary in sec. 2.1.3 'Key phonological alternations', p. 9
catalog_quote: Unlike the metrical system of a language like English, where there is a clear rhythmic pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables, Tommo So’s metrical structure is rather vaporous. However, certain phonological rules suggest a stem-initial strong-weak trochee [σ́σ̆]. This trochaic pattern does not continue throughout longer words – there is no sense of undulating rhythm as in a typical stress language. There is only evidence for this single foot, which comes from the following: 1. Vowel reduction to a high vowel or schwa in σ2 position [(C)VCV] 2. Post-sonorant syncope [(C)VRV] 3. /g/ spirantization [(C)VgV] ... I argue that these medial high vowels arise from the metrical system of Tommo So, where the second syllable, particularly in longer words (3+ syllables), is a metrically weak position. It receives less emphasis than the syllables around it, and hence this position is prone to vowel reduction.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tommo So is a tone language (H, L, extensive grammatical tone overlays) with no audible rhythmic stress; the only metrical structure the author finds is a single left-aligned (stem-initial) trochee: the first syllable of the stem is strong and the second syllable is weak (it undergoes vowel reduction to a high vowel/schwa, post-sonorant syncope in verbs, and /g/ lenition), 'particularly in longer words' (p. 9, p. 66-67: 'no weakening is ever found in syllables other than the second syllable'). If coded positionally this is stem-initial prominence, but the author explicitly declines to call it a stress system.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: 'This trochaic pattern does not continue throughout longer words – there is no sense of undulating rhythm'; only one foot per stem. (The 2010 draft, sec. 3.2.3, notes that long words/crypto-compounds behave as compounds, 'generally but not always split into two trochees [σ́σ̆-σ́σ̆]', i.e. each compound member has its own initial trochee.)
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllabic words may have a long vowel in the second syllable, so the weak-σ2 restriction is operative mainly in longer words (p. 43 snippet); post-sonorant syncope applies only in verbs and verbal nouns and only to the 2nd syllable of CVCV stems before coronal-stop suffixes (p. 67); a few /LHL/ trisyllabic nouns are Fulfulde loans whose tone pattern reflects Fulfulde stress (p. 86 snippet).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the stem (stem-initial trochee), not the phonological word or phrase; evidence is segmental (reduction/syncope/lenition), not pitch or perceived prominence; tone is lexical/grammatical and independent of this foot.
new_statements.identity_note: McPherson's description is based mainly on the Tédié (Tédjé) commune variety of Tommo So on the Bandiagara-Douentza plateau (grammar p. 9 names Tédié speakers); language-level glottocode tomm1242, no separate dialect code needed. The 2010 draft spells the language 'Tɔmmɔ-Sɔ'.

tone_statements.citation: McPherson, Laura. 2019. The role of music in documenting phonological grammar: Two case studies from West Africa. In Proceedings of the 2018 Annual Meeting on Phonology (Proceedings of the Annual Meetings on Phonology 7). Washington, DC: Linguistic Society of America. doi:10.3765/amp.v7i0.4493.
tone_statements.quote: For background, Tommo So has two contrastive tonal primitives, H and L, which can combine to form the contour tones HL and LH on heavy syllables. Minimal pairs contrasting H and L are shown in (1): (1) a. /H/ dámmá /LH/ dàmmá village hoe b. /H/ ísé /LH/ ìsé empty dog In addition, syllables may be surface-underspecified for tone … native vocabulary shows primarily two lexical tone melodies: /LH/ (rising) and /H/ (non-rising); falling melodies /HL/ make up only 6% of nouns, most of which are loanwords from Fulfulde.
tone_statements.locator: p. 2, sec. 3 'Case study 1: Tommo So tonal textsetting' + p. 5, sec. 3.3
tone_statements.summary: Two contrastive tones, H and L, forming HL and LH contours on heavy syllables; some syllables surface-toneless; lexical melodies mostly /LH/ and /H/; replacive grammatical overlays; heavy downdrift.

tone_statements.citation: McPherson, Laura and Ryan, Kevin (2018). Tone-tune association in Tommo So (Dogon) folk songs. Language 94. pp. 119-156.
tone_statements.quote: In terms of tone, Tommo So has two tonal primitives H and L, which can combine to form the contour tones LH and HL. Lexical tone melodies are very constrained, with nearly all native vocabulary falling into one of two melodies, /H/ and /LH/. … /HL/ lexical melodies are rare in native vocabulary but fairly common in loanword vocabulary … Regardless of the overall melody, all lexical stems must bear at least one H tone. In addition to H and L, Tommo So has surface-underspecified syllables that receive their f0 contour by interpolation from surrounding tones (McPherson 2011).
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones, H and L, combining into LH and HL contours; native words take /H/ or /LH/ melodies (/HL/ in loans), every stem has an H; toneless clitics interpolated; tonal overlays; downdrift.

tone_statements.citation: McPherson, Laura & Jeffrey Heath. 2016. Phrasal grammatical tone in the Dogon languages: The role of constraint interaction. Natural Language & Linguistic Theory 34(2): 593-639 (online 26 Aug 2015).
tone_statements.quote: Tommo So has three lexical tone patterns for non-verbal stems,3 /H/, /LH/, and /HL/, all of which are replaced by {L} when preceding an adjective … Like all Dogon languages, it has a phonemic distinction between L and H tone, though it additionally shows surface underspecified syllables (Ø), which receive F0 through interpolation (McPherson 2011). Importantly, almost all Dogon languages have a ban on lexically /L/ words; this means that the most common overlay, {L}, is always audibly distinct from lexical tone.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 1.1 'The problem', ms p. 3 and sec. 2 'Dogon languages', ms p. 5
tone_statements.summary: Two phonemic tones, H and L, with some surface toneless syllables filled by interpolation; noun stems carry /H/, /LH/ or /HL/ (verbs H vs LH), never all-L; NP modifiers impose {L}, {H}, {HL} overlays.

tone_statements.citation: Heath, Jeffrey & McPherson, Laura. 2013. Tonosyntax and reference restriction in Dogon NPs. Language 89(2): 265-296. doi:10.1353/lan.2013.0020
tone_statements.quote: In Ben Tey and the other languages in our sample, open-class stems (noun, adjective, numeral, verb) must have at least one lexical H-tone. Using /…/ to enclose lexical tones, stems may be lexically /H/, /LH/, /HL/, /LHL/, or (rarely) /HLH/, but (using # for ungrammatical) not #/L/. A consequence of this is that the most common overlay {L}—that is, stem-wide tone-lowering—is always overt (audible). … In Tommo So, possessive enclitic =mɔ is optionally attached to a preposed possessor … The possessor-controlled overlay in this language is {L}, so the formula without the enclitic is [Poss LN].
tone_statements.locator: p. 268, end of sec. 1.3 + p. 287, sec. 7.3
tone_statements.summary: Tone built from H and L only: every stem carries one of five lexical melodies /H/, /LH/, /HL/, /LHL/, rarely /HLH/ (never all-L; n = melodies); in NPs possessors and modifiers impose an {L} overlay.

tone_statements.citation: McPherson, Laura. 2013. The structural origins of tonal overlays in Tommo So (Dogon) compounds. Journal of West African Languages 40(1).
tone_statements.quote: Tommo So is a two-tone language, and the only licit stem melodies for native words are /H/ and /LH/.2 … Given these two lexical tonal melodies (with a few exceptional cases of /HL/ introduced from loanwords) … 2 Tone melodies in slashes indicate a stem-level lexical melody, which is mapped onto any number of available moras, though not in an automatic fashion. That is, a melody /LH/ can be realized on a trisyllabic stem as either LLH or LHH, as in kɛb̀ ɛl̀ ɛ́ ‘shard’ and kògódó ‘shell’. This is contrast to melodies in curly brackets (e.g. {L}), which indicate grammatical overlays.
tone_statements.summary: Two tones, H and L; native stems carry a melody /H/ or /LH/ (rare /HL/ in loans) mapped over the moras; grammatical {L} overlays erase stem tone in compounds and modified NPs; no floating tones.

tone_statements.citation: Sande, Hannah, Peter Jenks & Sharon Inkelas. 2020. Cophonologies by Ph(r)ase. Natural Language & Linguistic Theory 38(4): 1211-1261. doi:10.1007/s11049-020-09467-x
tone_statements.quote: In Dogon languages, certain modifiers within a noun phrase (DP) assign a tone melody to other elements inside that DP (McPherson 2014; McPherson and Heath 2016). For example, an inalienable possessor assigns a H(L) tone to its right (the noun), and an adjective assigns a L tone to its left (the noun). [...] in Tommo So the tonal requirements of the Mod head surface, and the H(L) tone assigned by the possessor is suppressed. This results in the noun surfacing with a L tone, rather than the possessive-assigned H(L) or the noun's lexical tone. The tone of the possessor is unaffected.
tone_statements.check: quotation from a journal article located by the 2026-09-24 journal search, not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: Inalienable possessors put a H(L) overlay on the following noun and adjectives put a L overlay on the preceding noun; when both are present in Tommo So the adjective's L wins on the noun and the possessor keeps its tone. Secondary data from McPherson 2014 and McPherson & Heath 2016, modelled with MaxEnt weights; matches the catalog's grammatical-overlay entry.

sources.citation: McPherson, Laura. 2010. A Grammar of Tɔmmɔ-Sɔ, Dogon Language Family, Mali. Draft dated 9/28/10 ('not finished or definitive'), UCLA, 262 pp. (precursor of Glottolog's 2011 draft, ref 301752, and of the 2013 Mouton grammar); formerly at dogonlanguages.org/docs/
sources.note: Sec. 3.2.2 'Metrical structure' (pp. 15-16): same statement in earlier wording: 'Unlike the metrical system in a language like English.. Tɔmmɔ-Sɔ's meter is rather vaporous. That being said, certain phonological rules suggest an underlying metrical structure, with a stem-initial strong-weak trochee [σ́σ̆]. This trochaic pattern does not continue throughout longer words—there is no sense of undulating rhythm as in a typical stress language. There is but one initial trochee.' Sec. 3.2.3 adds that crypto-compounds are 'generally but not always split into two trochees [σ́σ̆-σ́σ̆]'.

sources.quote: There are two tonal primitives L and H, which, in nominal elements, combine to form stem-level tone melodies {LH} and {H} on native lexical items. [...] In this thesis, I have demonstrated that Tommo So has a three-way tonal contrast of H, L and Ø, and this contrast persists all the way to the surface. The surface form of Ø is entirely predictable based on context, as it is assigned an F0 contour by interpolation between the preceding and following specified tones. Both lexical and boundary tones are able to serve as endpoints of interpolation.
